855.title: Stri: Gandhari's curse
855.hook: a man hangs upside down in a well, a serpent below, an elephant above, and he reaches for a drop of honey
855.howItsDone: Vidura's parable of the man in the well is retold in Hindu teaching and storytelling as a picture of life held between time and desire.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the night book, Sauptika, ended by the Ganga, with two sages between the weapons and a jewel carried home to Draupadi. Your line was a jewel carried home to a grieving mother.

A traveler is lost in a thick forest full of wild animals. Running from them, he falls into a well, but he doesn't hit the bottom. Creepers catch him, and he hangs there, upside down. Below him waits a great serpent. Above him, at the well's mouth, stands a dark elephant. Rats are gnawing at the roots of the tree that holds the creepers. And from a honeycomb in the branches, a drop of honey falls toward his mouth. This is how Stri, the book of the women, begins: with Vidura telling a story to a grieving king.
screen: `A MAN HANGS IN A WELL.` → `A SERPENT BELOW.` → `A DROP OF HONEY.`

segments.voice: The war is over. In Hastinapura, the old blind king Dhritarashtra has heard that Duryodhana and his brothers are dead, and he falls to the ground in grief. His half-brother Vidura, the wise one who warned him again and again, sits with him, and instead of an argument, he tells a story: the man in the well. In Ganguli's telling, what does the man do, hanging between the serpent and the elephant, with the rats chewing the roots? He drinks the honey, and he wants more. He still wishes to live, and he still wants the sweetness. Then Vidura explains. The forest is the world we wander in. The wild animals are illnesses. The well is the body. The serpent at the bottom is Time, which takes everything. The elephant is the year; the rats are the days and the nights eating away at our time; the creepers are the hope of life that holds us. The honey is the pleasures we keep reaching for, even here. Vidura isn't mocking the man. He's describing everyone, the king included. His counsel is gentle and hard at once: every living being comes to this; grief cannot bring your sons back; let the wise not be swept away by it. Before the women walk out onto the field to find their dead, the story pauses on a man in a well, still tasting the honey.
screen: `THE KING HEARS THE NEWS` · `VIDURA TELLS A STORY` · `HE STILL WANTS THE HONEY` · then, large: `THE WELL IS THE WORLD`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Stri opened with Vidura's story for a grieving king: a man in a well, still reaching for the honey.

A line of chariots and carts leaves Hastinapura, and behind it walk the women of the royal house, weeping, their hair unbound. They're going out to the battlefield to find their dead. At the front is Dhritarashtra, the blind old king, with Gandhari beside him. On the road, the Pandavas come to meet him: the five brothers who won, with Krishna. They bow. The king has to greet them. And he asks for one of them in particular.
screen: `THE WOMEN WALK OUT.` → `THE PANDAVAS COME TO MEET HIM.` → `HE ASKS FOR ONE.`

segments.voice: Dhritarashtra embraces Yudhishthira first, the text says, without joy. Then he asks for Bhima, the one who killed Duryodhana and Duhshasana, who made the vows and kept them. Krishna understands what's in the old man's heart. He quietly pushes Bhima aside and moves forward an iron statue of Bhima, which Duryodhana had made, in Ganguli's telling, to practice against with his mace. The blind king takes the iron figure in his arms and crushes it. He's so strong, and so full of grief and rage, that the statue breaks apart, and he hurts himself doing it. He falls to the ground, and Sanjaya lifts him up. Then Dhritarashtra weeps, crying out for Bhima, sure he has just killed him. Krishna speaks. It was not Bhima, he says, in effect. It was an image of iron. I knew what you meant to do. Your sons died because of their own deeds and because you didn't stop them. The king is ashamed, and maybe relieved. He washes, and then he embraces the brothers, Bhima too, with blessings this time. Look at the order of things. A father's grief is so strong it could kill. Krishna doesn't shame him in front of everyone or refuse the embrace. He gives the grief something to break that isn't a person. Only after it breaks can the real embrace happen.

segments.voice: Yesterday in Stri, the blind king crushed an iron Bhima, and only then embraced the living one. Your line was only an image of iron.

The winners of the war have a visit to make, and nobody wants to make it. The five Pandava brothers, with Krishna beside them, have to stand in front of Gandhari, the queen whose sons fell to them on that field. She has kept her eyes bound with a cloth for her whole married life, the story says, and her years of discipline have given her a power the brothers fear. Her anger could burn. Before they arrive, the sage Vyasa comes to her first.
screen: `THE WINNERS MUST VISIT.` → `A MOTHER WITH BOUND EYES.` → `VYASA COMES FIRST.`

segments.voice: Vyasa reminds Gandhari of her own words. All through the war, when Duryodhana came asking for her blessing, she gave him the same answer: where dharma is, there victory is. She never blessed him with victory. Now, Vyasa says, the words have come true. Don't let anger undo them. So she holds the curse back, but she has a question for Bhima. Why did you strike my son below the navel, against the rules of the mace fight? Bhima doesn't pretend. In Ganguli's telling, he says he was afraid, that Duryodhana could not be beaten fairly, and he reminds her what her son did to Draupadi in the hall. Then the harder question: did you really drink Duhshasana's blood? It never passed his lips, Bhima answers. Then Gandhari asks for the king. Yudhishthira comes forward, trembling, hands joined: I killed your sons. Curse me. Gandhari says nothing. But through a small gap in the cloth, her gaze falls on the tips of his toes, and his nails, fine a moment before, turn dark and damaged. Arjuna, watching, steps behind Krishna. Then her anger passes. She comforts them the way a mother would and sends them to their own mother, Kunti. One look through a sliver of cloth, and that's all the burning there is. The book is named for women, and here a woman holds the power to burn the winners, and mostly chooses not to use it.

858.title: Stri: Gandhari's curse
858.hook: the queen who chose not to see is given sight, and the first thing she sees is the battlefield
858.howItsDone: Gandhari's lament on the battlefield, spoken to Krishna, is read and retold as a passage of mourning, and some modern plays and poems take it up.

segments.voice: Yesterday in Stri, Gandhari held back her curse, and only one glance through her blindfold escaped. Your line was that's all the burning there is.

For years Gandhari has lived behind a cloth she tied on herself. Now the sage Vyasa gives her what the text calls a celestial sight, a way to see far beyond where she stands. She doesn't turn it on the sky, or the palace, or the faces of the Pandavas. She turns it on the field of Kurukshetra, where the war just ended. And beside her stands Krishna, the one person she will speak to about all of it.
screen: `A CLOTH SHE TIED HERSELF.` → `VYASA GIVES HER SIGHT.` → `SHE LOOKS AT THE FIELD.`

segments.voice: What she sees first isn't warriors. It's women. Wives, mothers and daughters of both armies move across the field, searching. Some have never walked outside the women's quarters before, and now they're out among the dead, hair loose, calling names. Stri means woman, and here the epic hands the women the story. Gandhari describes it all to Krishna, scene after scene. She sees Uttara, the young widow of Abhimanyu, Arjuna's son, bending over him and talking to him as if he could still hear. She sees her own daughter, Duhshala, running here and there, looking for her husband Jayadratha and unable to find his head. She sees her son Duryodhana on the ground, and his wife beside him. She sees Karna, and the women grieving him too. And she keeps turning to Krishna. Look at this, she says. Look at her. She isn't counting victories or losses for one side. The women come from both camps, and their grief sounds the same: a Pandava widow and a Kaurava widow, doing exactly the same thing in the dust. The war books spent chapter after chapter on who killed whom. Stri spends its time on who's left to bury them. Gandhari's grief will break by the end of her speech. Today she simply looks, and makes Krishna look with her.

859.title: Stri: Gandhari's curse
859.hook: a grieving mother turns to Krishna and curses him, and he answers with something close to a smile
859.carry: he takes it without striking back
859.howItsDone: Gandhari's curse on Krishna is told in temple discourses, plays and retellings of the epic, and storytellers link it to the later end of Krishna's own clan.

segments.voice: Yesterday in Stri, Gandhari was given sight and turned it on the women searching the field. Your line was look at this, she says.

She has been talking to Krishna the whole time. Look at this widow, look at that mother, look at my son. And somewhere in that long walk across the field, the grief turns. Gandhari stops describing and starts accusing. You could have stopped this, she tells him. You had the power. You had the words. Both sides listened to you, and you let it happen. The curse in this book's title isn't aimed at the Pandavas. It's aimed at Krishna, standing right beside her.
screen: `THE GRIEF TURNS.` → `"YOU COULD HAVE STOPPED THIS."` → `THE CURSE IS FOR KRISHNA.`

segments.voice: Gandhari reaches for the power her discipline has given her, the power she held back with Yudhishthira. Because you stood by while the Kurus and the Pandavas destroyed each other, she says, your own kinsmen, the Vrishnis, will kill one another. You yourself will die alone, in a wild place, by an inglorious means. And the women of your house will weep over their dead, the way the women of mine are weeping now. She has just spent this book looking at grieving women, and now she wishes that same scene on Krishna's family. Then the surprise. Krishna doesn't argue or defend the war. In Ganguli's telling he answers calmly, almost with a smile. I already knew this, he says, in effect. My people can't be destroyed by anyone else; they will destroy themselves. You've only spoken what was going to happen. Then he gently turns her grief back to her. The war came, he says, from your son's choices, and from your own failure to restrain him. Get up. Don't give yourself to sorrow. Gandhari falls silent. So the curse lands, and Krishna accepts it. The book doesn't settle whether she was right to blame him. It lets a mother say something almost unsayable to Krishna, whom the epic honors as God, and lets him take it without striking back. The epic will come back to this curse. For now, it hangs in the air over the field.

Water is the last thing the living can give the dead. After the fires on the field are lit, the whole household walks down to the Ganga: the Pandavas, Dhritarashtra, Gandhari, Kunti, the widows of both sides. One by one they step into the river and offer water for each person they lost, a father, a brother, a son, a teacher. A quiet, orderly rite after so much noise. And in the middle of it, Kunti tells her sons something she has carried their whole lives.
screen: `THE FIRES ARE LIT.` → `EVERYONE GOES TO THE GANGA.` → `KUNTI SPEAKS.`

segments.voice: Kunti asks her sons to offer water for one more warrior: Karna. The brothers are puzzled. Karna was the enemy, the charioteer's son, the man Arjuna killed. Why him? He was your eldest brother, Kunti tells them. My son, born to me from the sun god before I married your father. I set him adrift as a baby, and I never told you. The Pandavas are stunned. Yudhishthira is crushed. Soon after, as the next book opens, he remembers how Karna's feet resembled Kunti's, the text says, and how his anger used to drain away when he looked at them. Now he understands why. He grieves for the brother he fought without knowing, who, he realizes, could have been on his side all along. He offers the water for Karna himself, and brings Karna's family into the rites. The book of the women opened with a blind king's grief. It closes with a woman's word changing what the men thought the war was. Gandhari held back a curse, then spoke one. The widows walked the field. And at the river, Kunti turns the victory upside down: the warrior whose fall they had cheered was their own brother. That's Stri, a book where the women speak, and the winners learn what their victory cost.

861.hook: the man who won the war wants to walk away from the throne, so Krishna takes him to the grandfather he brought down
861.tomorrow: Shanti and Anushasana: Bhishma's teachings from the bed of arrows (selections)
861.howItsDone: Some Hindu teachers and students read the Shanti Parva and Anushasana Parva as a storehouse of teaching on duty, kingship and freedom, and the scene of Yudhishthira at Bhishma's side is painted and retold as the frame for all of it.

segments.voice: Yesterday Stri ended at the river, where Kunti told her sons that Karna was their brother. Your line was he was your eldest brother.

Yudhishthira has everything he fought for, and he doesn't want any of it. The kingdom is his. His enemies are gone. And he tells his brothers he's leaving for the forest, to live as a hermit. A kingdom bought with the deaths of teachers, cousins and a brother he never knew is not something he can bear to rule. His brothers argue. Draupadi argues. Sages come and argue, and at last he lets himself be crowned. But the grief and doubt don't leave him. So Krishna takes him to the field, to the one teacher still alive there: Bhishma, lying on his bed of arrows.
screen: `HE WON, AND WANTS TO LEAVE.` → `NOBODY CAN MOVE HIM.` → `KRISHNA TAKES HIM TO BHISHMA.`

segments.voice: These next two books, Shanti and Anushasana, are mostly one long conversation. Shanti means peace; Anushasana means instruction. The peace being sought is Yudhishthira's own, the peace of a man who can't live with what he's won. The surprise is who teaches. Krishna is there, and Krishna is God in this story. Yet he steps back. He gives Bhishma relief, so the pain of the arrows, the weariness and the confusion leave him, and his mind becomes clear, with all he ever learned ready to hand. Bhishma asks, in effect, why me? You could teach him yourself. Krishna's answer, in Ganguli's telling: he wants these words to come from Bhishma, so that Bhishma's fame will last as long as the world does. Then there's Yudhishthira. He hangs back, ashamed. His side brought this old man down, and he's afraid to come close. Bhishma has to call him forward and tell him he has nothing to fear. So look at the scene. A dying man on a bed of arrows. A ruler who can't forgive himself, asking the man he wounded how to live. And God standing to one side, letting the human being speak. Over the next days we'll take a few selections from what Bhishma says: about kings, hard times, guests, blame, and letting go. This week began with Vidura's man in the well, still reaching for the honey. It ends with a grieving king at a teacher's bedside.
screen: `SHANTI: PEACE. ANUSHASANA: INSTRUCTION.` · `KRISHNA GIVES BHISHMA CLARITY` · `YUDHISHTHIRA HANGS BACK` · then, large: `GOD LETS BHISHMA TEACH`

segments.voice: Let your shoulders drop and picture yourself sitting beside one person who taught you something real, a parent, a teacher, a friend, an elder. Breathe in and let one question you'd ask them now come up, with any shame or distance that's there too; you don't need the answer. If you pray, you can hold that person and your question in your prayer.
